scenes.narration: One hundred and sixty-six billion dollars. That is roughly how much the United States had charged in tariffs that the Supreme Court later said the President had no power to impose. The number is the customs agency's own estimate.

scenes.narration: Now the government is paying that money back. By late October, it had sent about one hundred and twenty-seven point seven billion dollars in refunds, with interest, to the Treasury for payment. But almost none of it is going to the people who paid higher prices in the store.
So who really paid those tariffs, and who is getting the money back?
By the end of this video, you will know how a tariff travels from a port to your shopping cart, how the refund machine works, and why the checks are going to companies, not to you.

scenes.narration: The tariffs were imposed under an emergency powers law known as IEEPA. Importers sued. On February twentieth, twenty twenty-six, the Supreme Court decided the case, Learning Resources versus Trump, by a vote of six to three.

The ruling was short and direct. In the Court's words, the emergency law does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the majority. Justices Thomas, Alito and Kavanaugh dissented.

But the decision left one huge question open. Justice Kavanaugh pointed it out in his dissent. The Court, he wrote, said nothing about whether or how the government should return the billions it had collected from importers. He predicted it would likely be a mess. And he added a line that sits at the heart of this story. Some importers may have already passed on the costs to consumers.

The scale was enormous. According to the customs agency's estimate, those tariffs had been charged on fifty-three million import shipments, paid by about three hundred and thirty thousand different importers.

Let me draw who pays a tariff. Here is a factory abroad. Here is the American company that imports its goods. The tariff is charged at the port, and the importer pays it to customs. Then the goods go to a store, and to you. The law sees only the first payment. Your price tag is a separate story.

scenes.narration: So the legal question was settled. The money question was just beginning. And the first part of it is simple. Who actually paid?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: On paper, the importer pays. That is how a tariff works. A company brings a shipment of toys or shoes into the country, and before customs releases it, the company pays the duty. The government never sends you a bill.

But companies do not have to keep that cost. They can raise their prices. Economists measure this with a number called pass-through. Researchers at the Yale Budget Lab estimate that for everyday core goods, between forty-six and eighty-six percent of the tariffs showed up in consumer prices, depending on how you measure it.

Researchers at the New York Fed found something similar, but slower. They estimate that nearly ninety percent of the twenty twenty-five tariffs passed through into the prices of imported goods. The effect on store prices built up more gradually, over many months.

So the honest answer is that the cost was shared. Importers paid customs first. Then many of them passed a large part of it on, to stores and to shoppers. Exactly how much reached you depends on the product and the company, and no one can trace every dollar.

Let me draw a tariff dollar. One dollar goes to customs. Part of it stays with the importer as a lower profit. Part of it moves down the chain, into the wholesale price, then the store price. By the time it reaches your receipt, it is hidden inside the price of a sweater or a toaster.

scenes.narration: The customs agency built a new refund system inside its import software. It opened in stages. First, in April, for recent shipments. Then, in June, for more complex cases. And in October, for the oldest shipments, but only for importers that had gone to court and won an order.

That last step pushed thousands of companies into court. More than four thousand cases were filed at the trade court in New York, many of them simply to get the court order that the refund system requires.

The money moved fast. By the end of July, the agency said it had sent about one hundred billion dollars in refunds, including interest, to the Treasury for payment. By late October, the total reached one hundred and twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.

You can see it in the Treasury's own books. In June twenty twenty-six alone, customs refunds were about forty-nine billion dollars. For three months, from May to July, refunds were so large that the government's net customs revenue actually went negative.
And some money is simply waiting. About about nine hundred and ninety million dollars was on hold, because the importers had not yet given the government their bank details.

Let me draw the refund pipe. On the left, the customs agency, checking each shipment. In the middle, the Treasury, paying out. On the right, the importer's bank account. There is no pipe that leads to a shopper. The system was built to find the company that paid at the port, and only that company.

scenes.narration: The customs agency is blunt about it. It can only refund the duties to the importer of record, the company named on the import paperwork. There is no government refund for consumers. If you paid more for a toaster or a pair of shoes in twenty twenty-five, there is no form you can fill out to claim your share from the government.

Look at the retailers' own filings. Target reported nine hundred and ninety-four million dollars of tariff refunds in one quarter, booked as a reduction in its cost of sales. In plain words, the refund made its costs lower, and its profit higher.

keyframes.cue: of tariff refunds in one quarter

scenes.narration: Costco said it paid about five hundred million dollars in these tariffs and had received about three hundred and thirty-nine million back. It said part of that money was being invested in lower prices for its members. The clothing maker lululemon received one hundred and thirty-four point five million dollars, which lifted its gross margin. And the toy maker Mattel said it received eighty-eight million dollars, which helped push its gross margin to almost fifty-five percent.

The most direct case is FedEx. In its latest quarterly filing, FedEx said it had received about three point three billion dollars in refunds, and recorded about two point seven billion dollars as money owed back to those customers.

Let me draw three ways a refund can go. Some becomes profit, and shows up in a better quarter. Some goes back to business customers, like the shippers paying their clients. And some may turn into lower prices. Which one happens is up to each company.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which is exactly why shoppers are now going to court.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Consumers have filed class actions against several big companies. Costco disclosed four of them, which allege that tariffs were passed on to members through higher prices and should now be refunded. FedEx disclosed fourteen. These are allegations, and the cases are still going on.

The one class action a court has actually certified so far is different. In October twenty twenty-six, the trade court certified a class of importers, the companies that paid the duties, so that all of them can claim their refunds together.

Meanwhile, the tariffs did not simply disappear. Days after the ruling, the President used a different law, Section one twenty-two, to impose a ten percent surcharge for one hundred and fifty days. When it expired in July, new tariffs followed under yet another law, Section three oh one, on sixty economies. The Tax Foundation, a think tank, still estimates the tariff burden at about eight hundred and twenty dollars per American household in twenty twenty-six.

Let me draw the loop. Tariffs go in at the port. Prices rise on the shelf. The court says the tariffs were illegal. Refunds come out, to the importers. And new tariffs start the loop again, under a new law.

scenes.narration: So who actually gets the tariff refund? The companies that paid at the border. Not because anyone planned it that way, but because a tariff is legally a tax on the importer, even when the shopper ends up paying much of it. The money left through the port, and it is coming back through the same door. What each company does with it next is the part you can still watch. So the next time a price tag rises because of a tariff, remember where that money really travels. It leaves through your receipt, and if it ever comes back, it comes back to whoever paid at the port.
